News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 16:07:25 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category></category><title>French film star Depardieu drops appeal against sexual conviction</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261116-french-film-star-depardieu-drops-appeal-against-sexual-conviction</link><description>
French film star Gérard Depardieu on Monday dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women during the filming of a movie in 2021 and issued "sincere apologies" for his past behaviour on set. "For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour," Depardieu, 77, said in the statement, withdrawing his appeal on the day it was set to go to trial. "I believed my remarks and some of my gestures would be without consequences" for those involved, he said. "They were not, particularly coming from a powerful figure such as I once was."
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/381e507e-e1d3-11f1-8833-3f371022a770/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261116-153326-153510-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/381e507e-e1d3-11f1-8833-3f371022a770/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261116-153326-153510-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">3d0769ea-e1d3-11f1-a542-e5b24be31abb</guid><pubDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:51:39 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>French troops in Ukraine 'wouldn't be a surprise'</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261116-french-troops-in-ukraine-wouldn-t-be-a-surprise</link><description>
French soldiers have been operating in Ukraine for several months, training Ukrainian troops and helping maintain military equipment, France 24's sister radio network Radio France Internationale (RFI) reported on Monday. While the deployment has not been confirmed, such a mission would not come as a surprise to many in Ukraine, reports France 24's correspondent in Kyiv Gulliver Cragg.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d2585b3c-e1d1-11f1-8438-5f54d898a954/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261116-150424-150818-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d2585b3c-e1d1-11f1-8438-5f54d898a954/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261116-150424-150818-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">d7d2a540-e1d1-11f1-ba92-1da996bacd6c</guid><pubDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:49:56 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Prague: Thousands of Czechs rally against government media funding plan</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261116-prague-thousands-of-czechs-rally-against-government-media-funding-plan</link><description>
Tens of thousands of Czechs rallied in Prague on Sunday, November 15, against a government plan to cut a public media fee and move funding to the state budget, a policy critics say would dent the broadcasters' independence and viability.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5149e6e0-e1d7-11f1-9ee0-29048b396e03/w:1024/p:16x9/Prague.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5149e6e0-e1d7-11f1-9ee0-29048b396e03/w:1024/p:16x9/Prague.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">4efd8934-e1d5-11f1-893d-b5d9c55ce5e2</guid><pubDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:49:29 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Culture</category><title>Robert Pattinson named as new James Bond</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/culture/20261116-robert-pattinson-named-as-new-james-bond</link><description>
British actor Robert Pattinson, star of three mega-franchises, "The Batman", "Harry Potter" and "Twilight", has been named as the seventh 007. The announcement ends years of speculation about who would inherit the beloved role from Daniel Craig and comes five years after the last Bond release, "No Time to Die".
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/56be3f90-e1d2-11f1-92c9-3f371022a770/w:1024/p:16x9/000-C7FC3U6.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/56be3f90-e1d2-11f1-92c9-3f371022a770/w:1024/p:16x9/000-C7FC3U6.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">764e1e6c-e1d1-11f1-a47e-193f370e6aaa</guid><pubDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:43:18 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/56be3f90-e1d2-11f1-92c9-3f371022a770/w:1024/p:16x9/000-C7FC3U6.jpg">© Tiziana Fabi, AFP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><category>arts24</category><title>Melissa Auf Der Maur: 90s rock memoirs and photographs</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/arts24/20261116-melissa-auf-der-maur-90s-rock-memoirs-and-photographs</link><description>
Melissa Auf Der Maur grew up in Montreal, the daughter of a feminist activist mother and a journalist-turned-politician father. At just 22, she joined Courtney Love’s band Hole as its bass player, going on to become a role model for young female fans – and not only female fans – of alternative rock. She later joined The Smashing Pumpkins before striking out on her own as a solo artist. She dropped by FRANCE 24 to talk to Marjorie Hache about the epic decade that brought the 20th century to a close.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/f892c0ea-e1b2-11f1-b37c-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/CULTURE-16-11-2026-11-00-ING26-CLEAN-A-frame-52769.jpeg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/f892c0ea-e1b2-11f1-b37c-695cb59fade5/w:1024/p:16x9/CULTURE-16-11-2026-11-00-ING26-CLEAN-A-frame-52769.jpeg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">8198886c-e1b2-11f1-b931-5f2185daf696</guid><pubDate>Mon, 16 Nov 2026 15:17:10 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Marjorie HACHE</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years ]]> In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Odd detections at Colorado Springs

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Unidentified objects in orbit?

Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

"Echoes" from a 13,000-year-old satellite

Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

The STS-88 mission photographs

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

The legend continues

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

What is it?

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Why is it incredible?

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

]]> <![CDATA[ A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability ]]> We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."

As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."

Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

What is the Astra Carta?

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

What does the Astra Carta say?

"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

From paper to action

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page".

The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain"

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."

A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cachet of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

"If you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability.

Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.

NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating."

]]> <![CDATA[ 30 years ago, 'Space Jam' proposed the best way to resolve interplanetary disputes ]]> You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

]]> <![CDATA[ On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia ]]>

On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds.

When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use.

Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

Why it mattered

When the 300-foot telescope first debuted, it was not just the United States' largest radio observatory, but the largest such facility in the world. But its quick construction — just two years — led to it having to be significantly upgraded later.

"In 1970, the 300-foot’s surface had become so warped from maintenance crews, snow, and its own weight that a new finer-meshed aluminum surface was installed," the website for the National Radio Astronomy Observatory reads. "A larger traveling feed was also installed at the prime focus."

The collapse, however, was no one's fault. "Unforeseeable stress factors cracked a steel connector plate," wrote the NRAO.

During its years of observations, the 300-foot telescope contirbuted to the discovery of dark matter and the realization that pulsars come from supernova explosions.

"One of the most important products to come out of the 300-foot telescope was an all-sky survey of radio objects called the Green Bank 6cm Survey. Nearly every northern hemisphere radio object studied by any other telescope is from a catalog compiled using this telescope," reads the NRAO website.

Astronomers weigh in on what to expect ]]> For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

What is T. Coronae Borealis?

T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare?

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

What will happen when T CrB's nova light reaches Earth?

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Why is it so challenging to predict T. CrB's nova flare?

"T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the big hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

"The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold."

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

"There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption."

Hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain."

What will happen when T CrB's nova light reaches Earth?

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," said Schaefer.

Once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very quickly, in less than a day."

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," said Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. "

Where can I find the Blaze Star in the night sky?

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Having passed as close to Earth as it is going to get this time around on 12 October at a distance of 1.04 astronomical units or 97 million miles (156 million kilometres), the comet is currently magnitude +13 and fading. All eyes will be on 220P during its next time around the sun in late 2031.

Na zimu se přestěhovaly do nového zázemí ve Vesci</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/905851-ovecky-opustily-svahy-jestedu-na-zimu-se-prestehovaly-do-noveho-zazemi-ve-vesci.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/905851-ovecky-opustily-svahy-jestedu-na-zimu-se-prestehovaly-do-noveho-zazemi-ve-vesci.html</guid><pubDate>Sun, 15 Nov 2026 18:29:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Stádo deseti ovcí, které od června spásalo sjezdovku Skalka na Ještědu, se dnes přestěhovalo na zimní pobyt do libereckého Vesce. výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu dobrý den ze šluknovského výběžku, konce světa - šluknovský výběžek Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:12:33 +0000 cs hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.vybezek.eu/wp-uploads/2018/09/cropped-favicon-vybezek-32x32.png výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu 32 32 Starostovník 2026 https://www.vybezek.eu/295747-starostovnik-2026/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 11:41:02 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=295747 V termínu 9. a 10. října 2026 proběhly další komunální (a senátní) volby, Tudíž je čas na aktualizaci – snad už mají všichni na svých webech všechno správně.

Vlastně je to obdivuhodné (nebo spíš pozoruhodné?). Někde vážně stačí postavit jednu jedinou kandidátku a všechno je OK. Někde ostřílení matadoři zmizeli v propadlišti dějin a došlo k totální proměně. Někde opakují stále stejné chyby. Ale hlavně – pořád zůstává faktem, že spousta nespokojených a nadávajících nedokáže zvednout pozadí a zkusit cokoli dělat. Víte, že aby místní referendum bylo platné, musí se jej zúčastnit alespoň 35 %?

Dolní Podluží –

Dolní Podluží na FB:

DOLNÍ PODLUŽÍ MÁ NOVÉ VEDENÍ OBCE
Dnes proběhlo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva obce Dolní Podluží pro volební období 2026–2030.
Starostou obce byl zvolen pan Vít Nesnídal a místostarostou pan Jan Hampl.
Nově zvolenému vedení obce i všem členům zastupitelstva přejeme mnoho úspěchů, vzájemné spolupráce a správných rozhodnutí ve prospěch naší obce a jejích obyvatel.
Ať se Dolnímu Podluží daří i v dalších letech!

Jiříkov –

Město Jiříkov na FB:

NOVÉ ZASTUPITELSTVO JIŘÍKOVA ZAHÁJILO SVÉ VOLEBNÍ OBDOBÍ
(Jiříkovské noviny listopad 2026)
V pondělí 9. 11. 2026 se uskutečnilo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva města Jiříkov, které zahájilo nové čtyřleté volební období 2026–2030. Na programu bylo především složení slibu nově zvolených zastupitelů, volba vedení města a dalších orgánů samosprávy.
Po složení zákonem předepsaného slibu přistoupili zastupitelé k volbě starosty a místostarosty města. Starostou Jiříkova byl zvolen a svou funkci tak obhájil Ing. Bc. Jindřich Jurajda, DiS. (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA), který tak bude město zastupovat a řídit v dalších čtyřech letech. Funkci místostarosty bude nově vykonávat Ludvík Otradovský (Jiříkov 2030 – sportovci / hasiči / ODS).
Zastupitelstvo dále zvolilo členy Rady města Jiříkov. Jejími členy se stali Mgr. Michal Mrázek a Jaroslav Vöröš (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA) a Ing. Nikol Kopecká (Spolek přátel Jiříkova a Filipova). Součástí jednání byla také volba předsedů a členů finančního a kontrolního výboru. V čele finančního výboru usedla stejně jako v minulém volebním období Naděžda Stožická (NEZÁVISLÍ KANDIDÁTI MĚSTA JIŘÍKOVA) a předsedou kontrolního výboru se stal Mgr. Petr Kulhánek MBA (ANO 2011).
Nově zvolené vedení města tak přebírá odpovědnost za další rozvoj Jiříkova, hospodaření s městským majetkem, přípravu a realizaci investičních projektů i každodenní chod městské samosprávy.
Nové zastupitelstvo tvoří celkem 15 členů zvolených za čtyři kandidující uskupení. Jejich společným úkolem bude rozhodovat o důležitých otázkách života města a zastupovat zájmy jeho obyvatel.
Všem nově zvoleným zastupitelům přejeme hodně sil, trpělivosti a úspěchů při práci pro Jiříkov a jeho občany.

Na FB:

Krásná Lípa zvolila vedení města pro nové volební období

Dnes v podvečer proběhlo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva města Krásná Lípa. Do čela města bylo opět zvoleno dosavadní vedení. Starostou se stal Jan Kolář, první místostarostkou Jana Drobečková a druhým, neuvolněným místostarostou Zbyněk Linhart. V sedmičlenné radě města je doplní Karel Jarolímek, Jiří Podhorský, Jakub Melichar a Marek Simandl.

Nové volební období tak začíná ve znamení kontinuity a stability, s možností navázat na dosavadní práci a pokračovat v připravených projektech pro další rozvoj, ve prospěch města a jeho obyvatel.

Vážení spoluobčané, dne 4.11.2026 proběhlo ustavující zasedání Zastupitelstva města Mikulášovice pro volební období 2026 – 2030. Zastupitelstvo tvoří 11 zvolených zastupitelů, a sice Aleš Jandus, Dagmar Kalousková, Roman Nikolaus Klinger, Petra Muchová, Petr Opočenský, Dita Paťhová, Zdeněk Plešinger, Robert Riedel, Jana Šedová, Iveta Talian a Jan Tříško.

Předsedou kontrolního výboru byl zvolen zastupitel Robert Riedel a jeho členy Petr Pánek, Denisa Píchová, Petr Kalousek a Josef Hýbl.

Nově zvolené zastupitelstvo čeká řada úkolů, výzev i příležitostí. Důležitá bude vzájemná spolupráce, otevřená komunikace a naslouchání potřebám občanů. Společně budeme usilovat o další rozvoj našeho města, aby se nám zde dobře žilo. Děkujeme za důvěru.

Rybniště –

Obec Rybniště na FB:

Rybniště má nové zastupitelstvo!
V letošních komunálních volbách se o přízeň voličů ucházelo devět kandidátů z jediné kandidátní listiny – Hnutí nezávislých kandidátů pro rozvoj obce Rybniště.
Do sedmičlenného zastupitelstva obce byli zvoleni Ing. Roman Forfera, Bc. Petra Vojtěchová, Martin Weiner, Karel Masopust, Jakub Němeček, Jan Severin Solar a Mgr. Jaromír Rauch.
Na dnešním ustavujícím zasedání se všichni zastupitelé ujali funkce a bylo zvoleno vedení obce na další čtyři roky – nebo spíše potvrzeno to stávající. Starostou obce zůstává Ing. Roman Forfera a místostarostkou Bc. Petra Vojtěchová.
Budeme se snažit kormidlovat Rybniště ve stejném rytmu jako dosud. Věříme, že se nám společně podaří zase spousta hezkých věcí, které budou dělat Rybniště příjemným místem pro život.
Těšíme se na další čtyři roky!

Život jde dál:

Varnsdorfský minitrh? Za nás rozhodně povedená sobota!

Včera jsme vyrazili do Městské knihovny ve Varnsdorfu a rozhodně jsme tam nebyli jen do počtu! Roman představil svou už třetí pohádkovou knížku Mokré pohádky a my jsme s sebou přivezli také kousek našeho Život jde dál. Výrobky, na kterých se podíleli nevidomí a slabozrací, spoustu věcí k vidění i k zakoupení a hlavně chuť potkávat se s lidmi.

A že se jich u nás zastavilo! Někdo nakoupil, někdo si přišel popovídat, někdo nás podpořil jen svou přítomností. A přesně o tom to je. Každá taková podpora se počítá a každé milé setkání potěší.

Obrovské díky naší babče, Vlaďce Hermanové a Renatě Šimákové, které nám s tím vším pomáhaly. A samozřejmě děkujeme paní ředitelce za pozvání, milé přijetí a atmosféru, ve které se člověk cítí jako mezi svými.

Děkujeme všem, kteří za námi přišli, podpořili nás a udělali si čas. Bylo nám s vámi krásně!

Život jde dál a my jsme rádi, že jdete s námi.

Visit Varnsdorf:

Náš kraj má co vyprávět. A Regionální knižní minitrh to znovu potvrdil.

Za každou knihou je příběh. Za každým rukodělným výrobkem hodiny práce, nápadů a šikovných rukou. A za každou uchovanou tradicí člověk, kterému záleží na tom, aby nezmizela.

Právě takové bylo sobotní setkání s lidmi, kteří mají co říct, co předat a především chuť tvořit. S autory, kteří vydávají knihy a uchovávají příběhy našeho regionu. S tvůrci a řemeslníky, kteří vlastníma rukama vyrábějí originální věci, navazují na tradice a dávají jim nový život. Právě jejich práce, nápady a nadšení pomáhají udržovat místní kulturu živou a připomínají, jak bohatý a inspirativní náš kraj je.

Velké poděkování patří všem, kteří se na minitrhu představili. Ať už prostřednictvím svých knih, rukodělných výrobků, poctivé řemeslné práce nebo osobního příběhu. Děkujeme, že svou tvorbou obohacujete náš region a pomáháte uchovávat jeho jedinečnost pro další generace.

Poděkování si zaslouží také Městská knihovna Varnsdorf a celý její tým za skvělou přípravu, organizaci a příjemnou atmosféru, díky které se knihovna na jeden den proměnila v místo plné setkávání, inspirace a objevování.

A samozřejmě děkujeme všem návštěvníkům, kteří přišli podpořit regionální autory, tvůrce a prodejce. Každá zakoupená kniha, každý výrobek i každý zájem o místní tvorbu má svůj význam. Protože region netvoří jen místa a jejich historie. Především ho tvoří lidé. Ti, kteří něco vytvářejí, uchovávají, předávají dál a nenechávají příběhy našeho kraje zapadnout.

A právě takové setkání má smysl.
